answer: A café I am particularly fond of is a small, cosy place tucked away on a quiet street near my office in Sirajganj. I discovered it by accident about a year ago, when I ducked inside to escape a sudden monsoon downpour, and I have been a regular ever since. What makes it special is not just the tea, though their milk tea with a hint of cardamom is excellent, but the wonderfully [[inviting]] atmosphere. It has soft lighting, comfortable seating and quiet music, which makes it perfect for unwinding. There are only about eight tables, and the walls are decorated with old photographs of the town and the river. The staff are genuinely friendly and remember my usual order, which gives it a lovely [[personal touch]]. I usually have a cup of tea with a plate of singara, or a chicken sandwich if I have skipped lunch. I often go there to read or catch up with a friend, and I never feel rushed to leave. In a town where most places to eat are loud and crowded, finding somewhere so [[intimate]] feels like a real treat. The food is simple but consistently good, which is all I really want. Sometimes I even meet students from the consultancy there for an informal chat about their applications, because it is much more relaxed than the office. Honestly, it has become a bit of a second home, and I think a good café is [[worth its weight in gold]] for how [[welcoming]] it can be.

followUps.q: Do you prefer going to cafés alone or with friends?
followUps.answer: It depends on my mood. If I want to read or think, I go alone, but most of the time I go with a friend, because a café is really about good conversation as much as the tea.

followUps.q: Are cafés popular in your town?
followUps.answer: They are becoming more popular, especially among young people. Traditionally, people gathered at roadside tea stalls, which are still everywhere, but a few modern cafés have opened recently and they are usually quite busy.

note: Set in Sirajganj and 'city full of chains' changed to town; coffee became cardamom milk tea (he likes tea); added what he orders and meeting students; plain 'personal' mark widened to 'personal touch', added 'worth its weight in gold'.
